title: The Trachenko-Zaccone equation: nonlinear relaxation from glasses to complex systems
authors: Alessio Zaccone, Valeriy V. Ginzburg, Oleg V. Gendelman, Sofia F. Mauro, John C. Mauro
abstract: The Trachenko-Zaccone equation provides a compact nonlinear dynamical framework for describing non-Debye relaxation in disordered condensed matter. Originally developed to rationalize stretched- and compressed-exponential relaxation in liquids and glasses from the dynamics of interacting local relaxation events, the same equation has subsequently appeared in broader contexts, including polymer relaxation and nonlinear models of global population dynamics. This review retraces the conceptual development of the equation, with particular emphasis on its physical origin in Kostya Trachenko's feed-forward interaction mechanism, its mathematical structure, and its possible generalizations. We also include personal recollections of the work with Kostya Trachenko at Queen Mary University of London in August 2019, during which the equation emerged in essentially its present form. After reviewing applications to stress relaxation, glassy materials, polymer relaxation and population dynamics, we discuss future directions including time-dependent feedback parameters, coupled order parameters, heterogeneous and spatially resolved formulations, flux terms, network versions and stochastic extensions. The central theme of the review is that the Trachenko-Zaccone equation should be viewed not only as a model of glassy relaxation, but as a general nonlinear feedback equation with potential applications across complex systems.
summary: This review introduces the Trachenko-Zaccone equation as a unifying, nonlinear dynamical model for describing complex relaxation phenomena in disordered materials. It shows that this single equation can describe stretched, Debye, and compressed relaxation regimes based on the nature of the nonlinear feedback. The work elevates the equation from a specialized glass model to a general tool for complex systems dynamics.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of describing non-Debye relaxation in disordered condensed matter systems, moving beyond simple exponential decay laws.
main_result: It establishes the Trachenko-Zaccone equation as a general nonlinear feedback framework capable of unifying stretched, Debye, and compressed relaxation regimes.
method: The review traces the conceptual development of the equation, analyzing its mathematical structure and proposing extensions to incorporate spatial and temporal dependencies.
model_or_system: The core model is the Trachenko-Zaccone equation, applied to structural glasses, supercooled liquids, and polymers. It models relaxation as a nonlinear feedback process arising from local, interacting events.
key_observables: Relaxation functions, stretched-exponential decay, compressed-exponential decay, and the evolution of an observable $y(t)$ towards equilibrium.
important_parameters: The stretching exponent ($ eta$), relaxation time ($	au$), and the nonlinear feedback parameter ($K$) which dictates the relaxation regime.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the relaxation dynamics can be captured by a general nonlinear rate-feedback principle, which is then shown to encompass various physical limits.

paper_structure: The paper reviews the historical context (Debye vs. KWW), details the physical origin of the equation via Trachenko's mechanism, analyzes the mathematical structure, and concludes by discussing advanced generalizations like spatial and stochastic extensions.
why_interesting: The concept of nonlinear feedback governing relaxation rates is highly relevant to open quantum systems, particularly those exhibiting glassy dynamics or slow relaxation, suggesting a generalized framework beyond simple Markovian decay.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Historical evolution of the ideas leading to the Trachenko–Zaccone equation. Beginning with Kohlrausch’s empirical stretched-exponential relaxation (1854) and Debye’s theory of exponential relaxation (1929), progressively deeper physical understanding emerged through Frenkel’s kinetic theory of liquids [7], Phillips’ demonstration of the universality of stretched-exponential relaxation, and Trachenko’s feed-forward interaction mechanism for interacting local relaxation events. Figure 2. Experimental motivation for a unified description of stretched- and compressed-exponential relaxation. Normalized intensity-correlation functions measured by X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy in a metallic glass at different temperatures. The relaxation changes from stretched-exponential behaviour (β < 1) at higher temperatures to compressed-exponential behaviour (β > 1) at lower temperatures. The inset shows the corresponding temperature dependence of the exponent β, with the vertical line indicating the glass-transition region. Figure 3. Schematic representation of the two feedback mechanisms underlying the Trachenko–Zaccone equation. (a) Feed-forward hindrance in the stretched- exponential relaxation (SER) regime. Earlier concordant local relaxation events (LREs) redistribute stress onto regions that have not yet relaxed, progressively increasing the activation barrier V (n) for subsequent events. At the coarse-grained level this corresponds to V (n) = V0 + V1n/nr, and hence to K > 0. (b) Facilitation in the compressed-exponential relaxation (CER) regime. Figure 4. Numerical solutions illustrating the two non-Debye regimes generated by the Trachenko–Zaccone equation. For positive feedback parameter K > 0, the numerical solutions are accurately represented by stretched-exponential KWW functions with β < 1 (SER). For negative K < 0, the same evolution equation generates compressed-exponential relaxation with β > 1 (CER). The Debye law, β = 1, lies between these two regimes and corresponds to K = 0. The figure illustrates that stretched and compressed relaxation do not require separate phenomenological equations but emerge from opposite signs of the same nonlinear feedback parameter.

Figure 4 illustrates this result directly. The same first-order nonlinear equation produces relaxation curves that are well represented by KWW functions on either side of β = 1. The parameter K therefore provides a continuous dynamical coordinate connecting SER, Debye relaxation and CER.
